question: What does a piece gain by going back to the start?
intro: A bright D-major piece in two-beat bars: an eight-bar strain written out twice, then eight bars that lean onto the flat side, then the direction D.C. The alignment suggests that this performance goes back to the strain once and plays the flat-side bars again.

sections.label: A · the same eight bars, written out again
sections.mNote: melody repeated, with a changed final pickup

sections.label: B · flat-side bars, closing in D major
A · da capo, played once
sections.mNote: apparently resumes at bar 9; the written repeat is skipped

sections.label: B · the flat-side bars again
sections.mNote: second hearing; closes with the ritardando

cues.title: Semiquavers in both hands
cues.text: Two beats to the bar in D major, marked p. A tune sits on top of a stream of semiquavers shared between the hands, with bass notes on the beat. The mark at the head of the page counts quavers, at 132 to the minute.
cues.evidence: First edition p. 8 (IMSLP #03060): 2/4, p, two sharps, continuous semiquaver figuration with bass notes; metronome mark for quavers. The key is read from the score’s two-sharp signature and its D-major tune; the report’s global estimate is D major (r = 0.69), while its opening windows read A major (0:00) and F♯ minor (0:05–0:20), with 2.6–3.6 onsets per second at 0:00–0:25 and the loudest window at 0:10 (−6.5 dB).
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Slowing before the flat side
cues.text: Bars 14–15 carry a ritardando, marked rit. in the score, before the pickup that leads into the new eight bars. The report’s first strong boundary falls here, at about 0:28.
cues.evidence: Report: novelty 0.80 at 0:28, the first listed boundary. Provisional alignment: bar 14 at 27.6 s and bar 15 at 29.4 s. Score p. 9, first system: rit. in the last bars of the second eight. The report’s C natural among the top pitch classes at 0:30 (G B C) is consistent with chromatic bass notes there but is not used to name chords.

cues.title: Three titles in Italian
cues.text: A Florence edition, Scherzi Musicali, printed only three of the pieces and renamed them Rimembranza, Contentezza and Mistero: Nos. 1, 5 and 11. A Paris edition, Étrennes, had appeared in 1840.
cues.evidence: Robert-Schumann-Haus Zwickau, catalogue 175 Jahre Kinderszenen (2013), item 13: Paris edition Étrennes (1840) and the Florence Scherzi Musicali (c. 1845) with “Contentezza = Glückes genug”; item 14 records an unauthorised Dutch print.

composer.epithet: His music lets remembered fragments, concealed names and competing inner voices interrupt the forms that contain them.
facts: Piano with Friedrich Wieck; composition with Heinrich Dorn; extensive private study of Bach and Beethoven
Co-founder of the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik, 1834; editor until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
Leipzig Conservatoire teacher; municipal music director, Düsseldorf, 1850–53
composer.background:
Schumann grew up in Zwickau, where his father August was a bookseller and publisher. Reading and music developed together: Jean Paul’s novels, with their interruptions, doubles and changes of narrative voice, mattered alongside piano lessons. Sent to Leipzig to study law in 1828, he spent more time on music and literature; a period in Heidelberg did not reconcile him to a legal career. He returned to Leipzig to study piano seriously with Friedrich Wieck. Wieck’s daughter Clara, already performing publicly as a child, gave him an immediate example of the professional discipline he hoped to acquire.

A persistent problem with his right hand ended the prospect of a virtuoso career. The familiar account of a finger-strengthening device leaves the injury’s medical cause uncertain. Composition and criticism became his principal occupations. The early published piano works already had distinct literary and formal premises: the Abegg Variations derive a theme from letters, while Papillons relates its dances to the masked-ball ending of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre. The miniatures’ sudden juxtapositions recreate the experience of a narrative changing speakers and levels.
